problem: Natural language commands to indoor robots often contain positional ambiguity (e.g. 'go to the chair' when several chairs exist), and existing VLN/LLM navigation work does not resolve which object is meant via dialogue.
motivation: Robots can build accurate 3D/LiDAR maps and detect objects, but human commands are imprecise, so the robot may go to the wrong place. Multi-turn dialogue with an LLM/VLM can progressively narrow down candidates to a unique object that can be grounded in the map.
key_idea: A two-level mapping: a VLM maps dialogue to a unique object ID on ID-annotated snapshots (language-to-object), then depth and pose project that object onto the LiDAR map (object-to-map) for navigation.
insight: Separating language-to-object alignment from object-to-map alignment lets the VLM work over images with bounding-box ID tags, so it need only pick a tag. Performance depends on scene complexity: GPT-4o does well in simple rooms (Meeting room II AR 1) but is inconsistent in the classroom and cafeteria (e.g. Classroom-2 AR 0.4). Only GPT-4o handled multiple images, while concatenated images and sequential image rounds degraded other VLMs.
method: Level-1 mapping (object-to-LiDAR): robot rotates 360° taking 8 RGB-D snapshots, detects objects with YOLOv8, deduplicates and assigns unique IDs, gets masks from SAM, and projects mask pixels to the LiDAR map using depth, FoV and the robot pose (Eq. 1).
Annotated images: bounding boxes and object ID tags are drawn on the 8 RGB snapshots for the VLM.

Level-2 mapping (language-to-object): the first dialogue D1 goes to the LLM to parse time, position, object and action. If the position is ambiguous, later dialogues D_i and the annotated images go to the VLM, which answers 'The <object> is labeled as <ID> in the <which> image'. This repeats until unique or k is exceeded (failure).
Execution module: missions are placed in a scheduler and the robot is deployed with ROS commands to the mapped target position.
VisDia dataset and metrics: type-A (single target, progressively more clues) and type-B (ambiguous set narrowed down) dialogues across 5 spaces, scored with SR/AS/T_A and AR/NS/T_B.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) as LLM and VLM; YOLOv8 detector; SAM segmenter
setting.observation: RGB-D snapshots (8 views per position) + 2D LiDAR + offline LiDAR map
setting.action_space: navigation to a target map position via ROS (goal position)
setting.privileged: pre-built offline 2D LiDAR map (pre-exploration); ground-truth object centers used only for mapping-error evaluation

numbers_note: Custom VisDia benchmark, no standard navigation benchmarks. Table 1 lists only Classroom-1..4 and Cafeteria-1..3 (fewer than the described sequence counts); only selected rows are included here. No baselines compared.
results: GPT-4o resolves positional ambiguity well in simple spaces (T_A 0.86 in Office, T_B 0.913 in Meeting room II) but is inconsistent in complex ones (Classroom-2 T_B 0.5, Cafeteria-1 0.632). Level-1 mapping error averages 0.657 m (meeting room) and 0.983 m (office).
limitations: Depends on GPT-4o because it is the only VLM that handles multiple image inputs; open local VLMs fail with concatenated or sequential images
Accuracy drops in complex, cluttered scenes with many similar objects, and the object mapping error is large (max 4.9 m)
Small self-built dataset, no comparison with baselines; requires a pre-built LiDAR map and a scripted dialogue set
